summary: This standards-track memo defines ANAT semantics for the SDP grouping framework, which let alternative network address types, such as IPv4 and IPv6, be offered for one media stream. It was replaced by RFC 5245.

eli5.summary: A caller can say 'reach me at either of these kinds of addresses'. This lets one call offer old and new addresses. It was later replaced by RFC 5245.

questions: alternative network address types in sdp
subtitle: Let one media stream offer both IPv4 and IPv6 addresses.

tldr.problem: The Session Description Protocol (SDP) allows multiple codecs per media stream but only one network address, which breaks when clients support only IPv4 or only IPv6.
tldr.mechanism: ANAT (Alternative Network Address Types) adds a grouping semantic to the SDP grouping framework so one media stream can list multiple addresses of different types (IPv4 and IPv6), with a preference order.
tldr.outcome: A caller can offer both IPv4 and IPv6 endpoints for the same stream, letting both old and new clients use the same offer. RFC 5245 (ICE) later replaced this with a more complete solution that also handles NAT traversal.

today: RFC 5245 (ICE) supersedes this specification. ICE provides a more comprehensive solution that handles NAT traversal while also supporting alternative address types. RFC 4091 is now historic.

sections.title: Introduction
sections.content:
The Session Description Protocol (SDP) describes multimedia sessions. For each media stream (audio, video, etc.), an SDP offer specifies the codecs to use and a network address to send to. SDP allows multiple codecs per stream, but RFC 2327 specifies only one network address per 'm' line.

The problem arises when a caller wants to support both IPv4-only endpoints and IPv6-only endpoints. An IPv4-only device cannot accept an IPv6 address, and an IPv6-only device cannot use an IPv4 address. Without a way to offer multiple address types, a single offer cannot work for both.

This RFC defines the ANAT semantics for the SDP grouping framework. ANAT lets a session description group multiple media lines, each with a different network address type, to represent alternatives for the same logical media stream.
sections.eli5: A video call setup document normally says 'send video to this address'. But what if some people can only reach address type A and others only address type B? ANAT lets you say 'try address A first, but if that doesn't work, try address B'.

sections.title: ANAT and the Grouping Framework
sections.content:
The SDP grouping framework [RFC 3388] lets you bundle several media lines into a semantic group. Each group has a 'semantics' attribute that describes the relationship. ANAT defines a new semantics value: ANAT.

Media lines grouped with ANAT semantics all represent alternative network addresses for a single logical media stream. The entity generating the offer MUST be ready to receive (or send) media over any of the grouped 'm' lines. However, ANAT MUST NOT group lines whose network addresses are of the same type (such as two IPv4 addresses)—that is what the ICE protocol is for (see below).
sections.eli5: The grouping framework is like a label that says 'these lines go together'. ANAT is a label that says 'these are all ways to reach the same place, just different address types'.

sections.title: Scope and Relation to ICE
sections.content:
ANAT addresses different network address types (IPv4 vs IPv6). It is not designed for alternative transport addresses of the same type. Systems that need multiple addresses of the same type (for NAT traversal or redundancy) should use ICE (Interactive Connectivity Establishment) [RFC 5245] instead.

ICE encodes the primary address in the 'm' line and additional addresses as parameters below it. Endpoints that do not support ICE ignore those parameters and use only the 'm' line address. ANAT uses a different approach: it groups separate 'm' lines with different address types at the media grouping level, keeping IPv6 syntax separate from IPv4-specific NAT parameters. This yields syntax closer to vanilla SDP and avoids relegating IPv6 addresses to secondary status.
sections.eli5: Think of ICE as 'here's my main address, plus some backup ones'. ANAT is 'here are completely different address types to choose from'. They serve different purposes.

sections.title: Preference and Offer/Answer
sections.content:
When an offerer includes an ANAT group, the media lines in the group are listed in order of preference. The line listed first has the highest priority. An answerer receiving an ANAT group SHOULD use the address with the highest priority it understands, then set the ports of all other grouped lines to zero (disabling them).

When using ANAT with SIP, the offerer SHOULD include the sdp-anat option-tag in a Require header, signaling that ANAT support is needed.
sections.eli5: The order in the group list means 'try this one first'. If the other endpoint understands that type, great. If not, it picks the next one it can use and ignores the rest.

sections.title: Example
sections.content:
Here is a session description with an IPv6 address and an IPv4 address grouped using ANAT:

v=0
o=alice 280744730 28977631 IN IP4 host.example.com
s=
t=0 0
a=group:ANAT 1 2
m=audio 25000 RTP/AVP 0
c=IN IP6 2001:DB8::1
a=mid:1
m=audio 22334 RTP/AVP 0
c=IN IP4 192.0.2.1
a=mid:2

The a=group:ANAT 1 2 line groups the two media streams. The first line (mid=1) with the IPv6 address has higher preference. Both lines can include additional ICE addresses (a= lines) if needed.
sections.eli5: The SDP says 'I'm offering audio at either IPv6 address 2001:DB8::1 or IPv4 address 192.0.2.1'. The numbering (1 2) means try the IPv6 one first.
